    "body": "CryptoProvider is a public interface. Adding a new abstract method is a binary and source compatibility break for any implementation outside this repository compiled against an older Keycloak version; such providers will fail to compile or can throw AbstractMethodError when ServiceLoader invokes order(). Since this is only used to sort providers, it should have a default implementation (e.g. return 0)."

    "body": "detectProvider previously threw when more than one CryptoProvider was found. It now sorts only by order(), and DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200. If e.g. the default and FIPS provider are accidentally both on the classpath, ServiceLoader iteration order determines which one is used, so a non-FIPS provider may be selected in a FIPS environment instead of failing fast. Tie/conflict detection is still needed for providers with the same order, or the server providers need distinct precedence."

    "title": "getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider",
    "body": "The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning a BouncyCastle provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which on standard JVMs is typically SUN or SunJSSE, not BouncyCastle. Any code that uses the returned provider as a BC provider (for BC algorithms, adding it to Security, or looking up BC services) can get the wrong provider and fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException/NoSuchProviderException or use unintended crypto implementations."

For a DER INTEGER that does not fit in signLength/2 bytes, this discards significant high-order bytes instead of rejecting the malformed/non-canonical signature. That can turn an invalid oversized r or s into a different value and should throw an IOException unless the only extra byte is a leading zero sign byte."

findings.title: Adding abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public interface. Adding a new abstract method is a binary and source compatibility break for any implementation outside this repository compiled against an older Keycloak version; such providers will fail to compile or can throw AbstractMethodError when ServiceLoader invokes order(). Since this is only used to sort providers, it should have a default implementation (e.g. return 0).

findings.title: Equal-order server crypto providers are silently selected instead of rejected
findings.body: detectProvider previously threw when more than one CryptoProvider was found. It now sorts only by order(), and DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200. If e.g. the default and FIPS provider are accidentally both on the classpath, ServiceLoader iteration order determines which one is used, so a non-FIPS provider may be selected in a FIPS environment instead of failing fast. Tie/conflict detection is still needed for providers with the same order, or the server providers need distinct precedence.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as returning a BouncyCastle provider. This implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which on standard JVMs is typically SUN or SunJSSE, not BouncyCastle. Any code that uses the returned provider as a BC provider (for BC algorithms, adding it to Security, or looking up BC services) can get the wrong provider and fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException/NoSuchProviderException or use unintended crypto implementations.

findings.title: ECDSA DER-to-RS conversion silently truncates oversized integers
findings.body: integerToBytes copies only the low qLength bytes when BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than the field length. For a DER INTEGER that does not fit in signLength/2 bytes, this discards significant high-order bytes instead of rejecting the malformed/non-canonical signature. That can turn an invalid oversized r or s into a different value and should throw an IOException unless the only extra byte is a leading zero sign byte.

findings.title: ECDSA conversion tests only check round-trip symmetry
findings.body: The test signs data, converts DER to concatenated RS, back to DER, then back to concatenated RS, and only asserts the two raw RS arrays are equal. It never compares the reconstructed DER to the original signature or verifies the resulting bytes with Signature.verify. A pair of inverse bugs in the two conversion methods would pass. The test also uses the same default EC key pair for ES256, ES384, and ES512 instead of curve/key sizes matching each algorithm.
